title: Mental Health — Emergency II: Psychiatric & Medication Emergencies (Set 31)
subtitle: Phase-2 depth: recognizing psychiatric emergencies (suicide attempt in progress, violence, elopement of a high-risk client), responding to intentional overdose, and identifying psych-medication emergencies (NMS, serotonin syndrome, lithium toxicity, severe withdrawal/DTs, acute dystonia, anaphylaxis)—plus not mistaking a medical emergency (cardiac, low glucose, hypoxia) for 'just behavior,' scene safety, activating help within scope, and post-event documentation and debriefing
scenario: When minutes matter on a psychiatric unit: stopping a suicide attempt, responding to an overdose, spotting a medication emergency, refusing to write off chest pain or confusion as 'just anxiety,' keeping the scene safe, and getting the right help fast—within scope.

steps.q: A psychiatric emergency is BEST defined as:

opts.text: A situation involving imminent danger to the client or others that requires immediate intervention
opts.rat: Psychiatric emergencies involve imminent danger to self or others (such as an active suicide attempt or violence) and demand immediate action.

opts.text: Any client who is mildly upset about the schedule
opts.rat: Mild upset is not an emergency; an emergency involves imminent danger.

opts.text: A client who disagrees with a staff decision
opts.rat: Disagreement is not an emergency.

opts.text: Any request for extra attention
opts.rat: A request for attention is not, by itself, an emergency.

steps.q: A technician discovers a client actively attempting to harm themselves. The FIRST priority is to:

opts.text: Ensure immediate safety—stay with the client, call for help, and remove the means of harm
opts.rat: Immediate safety comes first: staying with the client, summoning help, and removing the means of self-harm.

opts.text: Leave to find paperwork before doing anything
opts.rat: The client is not left alone during an active attempt; safety and help come first.

opts.text: Wait to see whether the client is serious
opts.rat: An active attempt is acted on immediately, not observed for seriousness.

opts.text: Scold the client for the behavior
opts.rat: Scolding is nontherapeutic; the priority is safety and help.

steps.q: A client is found after an apparent attempt at self-strangulation and is now unresponsive. The technician should:

opts.text: Call for emergency help immediately, check responsiveness and breathing, begin indicated life support within training, and not leave the client
opts.rat: This is a medical and psychiatric emergency: activate help at once, assess airway/breathing, provide indicated BLS within training, and stay with the client.

opts.text: Assume the client is sleeping and walk away
opts.rat: An unresponsive client after a self-harm attempt is an emergency, not sleep.

opts.text: Document the finding and address it at the next shift
opts.rat: Immediate emergency response is required, not delayed documentation.

opts.text: Wait for the client to wake up on their own
opts.rat: Waiting risks the client's life; help is activated immediately.

steps.q: A client reports having intentionally swallowed a large amount of pills. The technician should:

opts.text: Activate help immediately, monitor responsiveness and breathing, save any container/pills to identify what was taken, and follow poison-control/medical guidance—without inducing vomiting on their own
opts.rat: Overdose is an emergency: get help, monitor airway and level of consciousness, preserve the substance for identification, and follow guidance—vomiting is not induced independently.

opts.text: Do nothing unless the client looks visibly ill
opts.rat: An overdose is acted on immediately, before deterioration.

opts.text: Make the client vomit right away without any guidance
opts.rat: Inducing vomiting can be dangerous and is not done independently; guidance is followed.

opts.text: Throw away the pill container to tidy up
opts.rat: The container is kept to help identify what was taken.

steps.q: A client on an antipsychotic develops a high fever, severe muscle rigidity, confusion, and unstable vital signs. The technician should recognize:

opts.text: Possible neuroleptic malignant syndrome—a medical emergency—hold the antipsychotic and report urgently
opts.rat: Fever, rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability suggest NMS, an emergency requiring the drug to be held and urgent reporting (see mh-core-25).

opts.text: A normal reaction that needs no action
opts.rat: These findings are an emergency, not a normal reaction.

opts.text: A reason to give another dose of the antipsychotic
opts.rat: More antipsychotic worsens NMS; the drug is held.

opts.text: A minor issue to mention next week
opts.rat: NMS requires urgent, immediate action.

steps.q: A client taking serotonergic medications develops agitation, fever, sweating, tremor, and overactive reflexes. The technician should suspect:

opts.text: Serotonin syndrome—a medical emergency—and report urgently
opts.rat: Agitation, fever, tremor, and hyperreflexia after serotonergic drugs suggest serotonin syndrome, which is reported urgently (see mh-core-25).

opts.text: A harmless side effect to ignore
opts.rat: These findings can indicate an emergency and are reported urgently.

opts.text: A reason to add another serotonergic medication
opts.rat: Adding serotonergic drugs would worsen the syndrome.

opts.text: Something to address only if it lasts a week
opts.rat: This is urgent, not something to observe for a week.

steps.q: A client on lithium develops a coarse tremor, vomiting, slurred speech, unsteady gait, and confusion. The technician should:

opts.text: Suspect lithium toxicity, hold the next dose, and report immediately
opts.rat: These are signs of lithium toxicity, an emergency; the dose is held and reported at once (see mh-core-24).

opts.text: Give extra lithium to steady the tremor
opts.rat: More lithium worsens toxicity; the dose is held.

opts.text: Assume it is unrelated to the medication
opts.rat: These findings strongly suggest lithium toxicity and are reported.

opts.text: Ignore it unless the client collapses
opts.rat: Toxicity is acted on early, not only after collapse.

steps.q: A client in severe alcohol withdrawal becomes confused and febrile with rapidly rising heart rate and blood pressure. The technician should recognize:

opts.text: A possible delirium-tremens emergency—report urgently, ensure safety, and maintain seizure precautions
opts.rat: Confusion, fever, and escalating vital signs suggest delirium tremens, a life-threatening emergency needing urgent reporting, safety, and seizure precautions (see mh-core-23).

opts.text: A minor stage that needs no monitoring
opts.rat: Severe alcohol withdrawal is potentially life-threatening and closely monitored.

opts.text: A reason to leave the client unmonitored
opts.rat: This client needs close monitoring and safety measures.

opts.text: Something to reassess next week
opts.rat: This is an urgent situation requiring immediate reporting.

steps.q: Shortly after an antipsychotic dose, a client develops a severe, sustained spasm of the neck and tongue and appears to have difficulty managing secretions. The technician should:

opts.text: Treat acute dystonia as an emergency—protect the airway, stay with the client, and call for help, anticipating an ordered medication
opts.rat: Acute dystonia can threaten the airway; airway protection, staying with the client, and urgent help (anticipating an ordered anticholinergic) are needed (see mh-core-25).

opts.text: Tell the client to relax and leave the area
opts.rat: This is an emergency; the client is not left, and help is summoned.

opts.text: Give the next antipsychotic dose early
opts.rat: More antipsychotic can worsen dystonia.

opts.text: Wait a few hours to see if it resolves
opts.rat: Airway-threatening dystonia needs immediate attention.

steps.q: A client suddenly develops hives, facial and lip swelling, and difficulty breathing after a medication. The technician should:

opts.text: Suspect anaphylaxis—activate emergency help immediately, monitor the airway and breathing, and follow orders/protocol (such as ordered epinephrine)
opts.rat: Swelling with breathing difficulty after a medication suggests anaphylaxis, a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate help and airway support per protocol.

opts.text: Assume it is a mild rash and do nothing
opts.rat: Airway swelling and breathing difficulty indicate an emergency, not a mild rash.

opts.text: Give the same medication again to confirm the reaction
opts.rat: Re-exposing the client would be dangerous.

opts.text: Wait until the swelling spreads further
opts.rat: Anaphylaxis is acted on immediately.

steps.q: A client suddenly reports crushing chest pain and looks pale and sweaty. The technician should:

opts.text: Treat it as a possible cardiac emergency—activate help, keep the client calm and resting, and report—rather than assuming it is 'just anxiety'
opts.rat: Chest pain with pallor and sweating can be a heart attack; it is treated as a possible cardiac emergency, not dismissed as anxiety.

opts.text: Assume it is only anxiety and take no action
opts.rat: Assuming anxiety can miss a life-threatening cardiac event; it is escalated.

opts.text: Tell the client to walk it off
opts.rat: Exertion during possible cardiac ischemia is dangerous.

opts.text: Wait until the next vital-sign round
opts.rat: Possible cardiac symptoms are acted on immediately.

steps.q: A client becomes acutely confused and agitated. Before assuming a purely psychiatric cause, the technician should consider that:

opts.text: A medical emergency—such as low blood glucose, low oxygen, or infection—can present as confusion or agitation, so these are assessed and reported
opts.rat: Medical problems like hypoglycemia, hypoxia, or infection can cause agitation/confusion; assessing and reporting them avoids missing a treatable emergency.

opts.text: Agitation is always purely psychiatric
opts.rat: Agitation can have medical causes that must be evaluated.

opts.text: Medical causes never present as behavior change
opts.rat: Medical emergencies frequently present as behavior or mental-status change.

opts.text: No assessment is needed if the client has a psychiatric diagnosis
opts.rat: A psychiatric diagnosis does not rule out a medical emergency; assessment is done.

steps.q: A client is choking during a meal, cannot cough, speak, or breathe. The technician should:

opts.text: Recognize a complete airway obstruction and act immediately with indicated interventions (such as abdominal thrusts), calling for help
opts.rat: Inability to cough, speak, or breathe signals complete obstruction; indicated interventions are started at once while help is summoned.

opts.text: Wait quietly to see if the client clears it alone
opts.rat: Complete obstruction requires immediate intervention, not waiting.

opts.text: Offer the client a drink of water
opts.rat: Giving fluids to a choking client is unsafe.

opts.text: Leave to get a supervisor before acting
opts.rat: Intervention begins immediately while help is called.

steps.q: A client at high risk for suicide suddenly bolts toward an exit in an apparent elopement attempt. The technician should:

opts.text: Treat it as a safety emergency—alert the team immediately, and take steps to keep the client from leaving unsafely while maintaining everyone's safety
opts.rat: Elopement of a high-risk client is a safety emergency; the team is alerted at once and the client is prevented from leaving unsafely, within safe limits.

opts.text: Allow the client to leave the unit alone
opts.rat: Letting a high-risk client leave alone is dangerous.

opts.text: Ignore it and continue other tasks
opts.rat: This is a safety emergency requiring immediate action.

opts.text: Wait to mention it at the next team meeting
opts.rat: The team is alerted immediately, not later.

steps.q: A client becomes physically violent and is attacking others. The technician's priority is to:

opts.text: Protect the safety of the client, other clients, and staff—summon the team/help, use de-escalation, and reserve physical intervention for imminent danger
opts.rat: Safety of everyone comes first: summon help, attempt de-escalation, and use physical intervention/restraint only as a last resort for imminent danger (see mh-core-11/28).

opts.text: Confront the client alone to prove control
opts.rat: Acting alone is unsafe; the team is summoned.

opts.text: Ignore the violence and hope it stops
opts.rat: Active violence is an emergency requiring immediate protective action.

opts.text: Punish the client afterward as the main goal
opts.rat: The goal is safety, not punishment.

steps.q: A severely agitated client is now also extremely exhausted, very hot, and physically deteriorating. The technician should recognize that:

opts.text: Extreme agitation with physical instability can be a medical emergency, so help is summoned and the client's safety and physical status are closely monitored
opts.rat: Severe agitation with hyperthermia and exhaustion can become a medical emergency; urgent help and close monitoring of physical status are needed, not just behavioral management.

opts.text: It is only a behavior problem with no medical risk
opts.rat: Severe agitation with physical instability carries real medical risk.

opts.text: The client should simply be left to tire out
opts.rat: A physically deteriorating client needs monitoring and help, not neglect.

opts.text: No monitoring of physical status is needed
opts.rat: Close physical monitoring is essential in this situation.

steps.q: Before approaching any emergency scene (for example, an agitated client who may have a weapon), the technician should FIRST:

opts.text: Ensure the scene is safe for themselves and others and get help, since a responder who is harmed cannot help
opts.rat: Scene safety comes first; a responder who becomes a victim cannot assist, so safety and help are ensured before approaching.

opts.text: Rush in immediately regardless of danger
opts.rat: Rushing into danger can create more victims; scene safety comes first.

opts.text: Ignore any potential weapon
opts.rat: Potential weapons are a serious safety concern that must be addressed.

opts.text: Approach alone without alerting anyone
opts.rat: Help is summoned; approaching a dangerous scene alone is unsafe.

steps.q: In any emergency, the technician's role is best described as:

opts.text: Recognize the emergency, activate the response/get help, provide care within their training and scope, and support licensed staff
opts.rat: The technician recognizes emergencies, activates help, acts within training/scope (such as BLS), and supports the licensed team—without exceeding scope.

opts.text: Perform advanced medical procedures beyond their training
opts.rat: The technician stays within scope and training, not performing advanced procedures they are not trained for.

opts.text: Wait passively for someone else to notice
opts.rat: The technician actively recognizes and responds to emergencies.

opts.text: Handle everything alone without calling for help
opts.rat: Activating help is a core part of emergency response.

steps.q: After a psychiatric emergency has resolved, an important technician responsibility is to:

opts.text: Document the event objectively and factually, participate in debriefing, and help restore a safe, calm environment for the client and others
opts.rat: Objective documentation, debriefing to learn and support, and restoring safety and calm are key post-emergency responsibilities.

opts.text: Avoid documenting to keep records simple
opts.rat: Accurate documentation of the event is required.

opts.text: Refuse to discuss the event in any debriefing
opts.rat: Debriefing supports learning and staff/client wellbeing.

opts.text: Leave the environment unsettled for other clients
opts.rat: Restoring a safe, calm environment is part of the response.

steps.q: Overall, the technician's approach to emergencies in the psychiatric setting is to:

opts.text: Ensure scene and personal safety, recognize both psychiatric and medical emergencies (never assuming 'just behavior'), activate help, intervene within scope, protect the client and others, and document and debrief—while medical management belongs to licensed staff
opts.rat: The technician keeps the scene safe, recognizes psychiatric and medical emergencies alike, activates help, acts within scope, protects everyone, and documents/debriefs, while medical management rests with licensed staff.

opts.text: Assume every acute change is purely psychiatric
opts.rat: Acute changes may be medical emergencies and are evaluated, not assumed psychiatric.

opts.text: Act beyond their scope in every situation
opts.rat: The technician acts within training and scope.

opts.text: Delay activating help to avoid disruption
opts.rat: Help is activated promptly; delay endangers the client.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: emergency recognition and response in the psychiatric setting (Phase-2 depth/application). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level and stated conceptually, marked for faculty confirmation: defining a psychiatric emergency (imminent danger to self/others); responding to an active suicide/self-harm attempt (stay, remove means, get help) and to an unresponsive client after an attempt (activate help, ABCs, BLS within training); intentional overdose response (activate help, monitor airway, preserve the substance, follow guidance, do not independently induce vomiting); recognizing psych-medication emergencies—neuroleptic malignant syndrome, serotonin syndrome, lithium toxicity, severe alcohol withdrawal/delirium tremens, acute dystonia (airway), and anaphylaxis—as urgent, cross-referencing the detailed sets (mh-core-23/24/25); not mistaking a medical emergency (cardiac chest pain, hypoglycemia, hypoxia, infection) for 'just anxiety' or 'just behavior'; complete airway obstruction/choking; elopement of a high-risk client and physical violence as safety emergencies (cross-referencing mh-core-11/28); severe agitation with physical instability as a potential medical emergency; scene and personal safety first; activating help and acting within training/scope (BLS); and post-emergency objective documentation, debriefing, and restoration of a safe environment—with medical management reserved to licensed staff. No specific drug doses, vital-sign cutoffs, or lab values are asserted here; qualitative recognition is used and the general first-aid/BLS, choking, seizure, shock, stroke, and chest-pain fundamentals are introduced in bnc-core-10. Builds on and does not duplicate bnc-core-10 (and the medication-emergency detail in mh-core-23/24/25). Pending faculty review.
